items.text: It uses neural fluctuations to explain masking phenomena that energy models struggle with, and employs manipulations such as equal energy and roving level to dissociate detection mechanisms; it does not premise its value on immediately producing a hearing aid.
It constrains models with individual cue usage and peripheral measurements, then predicts across tasks rather than fitting task by task, revealing individual differences within similar audiograms.

Computational modeling, human psychophysics, and awake-animal physiology mutually constrain one another and extend to spectral slope, consonant/spatial hearing; mechanistic knowledge can be gained even if the model is partially falsified.

Degrees of freedom such as peripheral damage, IC cell types, and readout noise/covariance raise issues of identifiability and model comparison; a distinction should be made between prior calibration and genuinely independent prediction.

Roving resistance does not uniquely demonstrate envelope cues, nor do equal-energy stimuli necessarily isolate a single mechanism; competing explanations need to be compared, and null results must be able to alter the hypothesis.

Bridging rabbit IC to human SNHL behavior and sampling neural populations have limitations; four chronic animals, 200 neurons per condition, and inconsistencies in human 40/45 affect feasibility and the precision of extrapolation.
